https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/ng-i.text: Over the past year and a half, at least 28 federal datasets have been deleted and another 338 data collections have been modified, according to dataindex.us. Illustration: Guardian Design/Getty Images View image in fullscreen Over the past year and a half, at least 28 federal datasets have been deleted and another 338 data collections have been modified, according to dataindex.us. Illustration: Guardian Design/Getty Images Deleted data US news Trump 2.0 has deleted or altered nearly 400 US datasets, endangering public health, education and more Health data appears to be most affected by administration’s attempt to wipe findings that don’t align with its priorities, tracker shows Building power is supported by About this content Amy Qin and Flávio Pessoa Tue 18 Aug 2026 06.00 EDT Last modified on Tue 18 Aug 2026 07.28 EDT Share A database of federal law enforcement officer misconduct records. A survey measuring physical, sexual and emotional violence against children and youth. Real-time pollution readings collected by air quality monitors from US embassies around the world. These are among the hundreds of federal datasets that the Trump administration has taken down or altered as part of its aggressive campaign to wipe all mentions of data findings that do not align with the administration’s priorities. Over the past year and a half, at least 28 federal datasets have been deleted and another 338 data collections have been modified, according to an online tracker released last week from dataindex.us , a group of data policy experts, researchers and developers that formed last year to monitor changes to government data. “We’re at a very vulnerable point as a nation,” said Denice Ross, former US chief data scientist under the Biden administration and a co-founder of dataindex.us. “We’re facing a future where we are not going to have the information that we need to make decisions that will save lives and benefit American communities.” The tracker includes detailed information about deleted or altered datasets from more than 60 federal agencies that span the environment, labor, law enforcement and other topics. But datasets on health appear to be the most affected by the Trump administration’s crackdown, comprising about 40% of the total number of terminated or altered data collections tracked by dataindex.us. Bar chart showing most common topics of federal data altered or deleted during Trump’s second term One of the main changes to these health datasets is that they no longer collect information on queer and trans people – as part of Donald Trump’s executive order “Defending Women from Gender Ideology Extremism and Restoring Biological Truth to the Federal Government”. Multiple Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) surveys, for example, have removed questions about respondents’ gender identity. These include the National HIV Surveillance System , the primary source of case data for HIV infections, the National Violent Death Reporting System , the CDC Diabetes Prevention Recognition Program , the National Intimate Partner and Sexual Violence Survey and specific surveys evaluating Prep uptake among gay men and in communities of color. In addition, there are at least four health datasets that are no longer being updated at all, including the Substance Abuse and Mental Health Administration’s (Samhsa) Drug Abuse Warning Network, a surveillance system that doctors and public health researchers used to track drug-related emergency room visits in near real-time to spot emerging overdose trends. “These data are critical for identifying emerging epidemics and what parts of the population are most vulnerable to different types of health conditions,” said Thomas Babor, a professor emeritus at the University of Connecticut who specializes in public health and addiction. “We need to know what direction the trend is going, whether it’s the beginning of an end; we need to learn from prior episodes of epidemics and how they were responded to and what impact the responses had,” Babor said. “Taking down, even temporarily, some of the most important surveys that we have, especially for comparative purposes, is like we’re erasing our institutional memory for public health.” Other deleted datasets include the US Department of Agriculture’s twice-annual survey of farm employers that counted the number of farm workers employed and their wages that informed the minimum pay rates for H-2A visa workers and a National Center for Education Statistics (NCES) survey of the pay and working conditions of teachers and principals at public and private schools across the country. Bar chart of agencies most affected by data deletion or alteration during Trump’s second term Christopher Dick, a co-founder of dataindex.us and former chief of the population evaluation, analysis and projections branch at the Census Bureau said they launched the online tracker because it was difficult to know exactly how many federal datasets had actually been deleted. Government agencies aren’t required to notify the public when data collections are terminated, and some datasets have simply stopped updating because of a lack of staffing while others have been quietly pulled from federal websites with little notice. Some federal datasets also change or update on a regular basis, so it can be hard to figure out what is actually permanently deleted compared with a regular update. “The question we’re trying to answer is: are certain datasets being taken away that have an impact on the American people?” Dick said. The group identified important deleted or altered datasets through a combination of research about how the dataset was used, crowdsourcing from media reports, government employees, and people who used the datasets, monitoring social media, and tracking notices posted about proposed regulations from the Office of Information and Regulatory Affairs. The dataindex.us tracker is not a complete list, and is probably still an undercount of all the deleted or altered datasets there are, said Ross. But the hope is the tracker is just a starting point. “We want people who depend on different datasets, some of which might be sort of obscure, to let us know what corners to look in because we don’t have full visibility,” Ross said. The Guardian’s Deleted data series explores how critical US government information is being deleted and what the consequences will be, and will preserve or recreate lost datasets. If you know about any datasets, webpages or government materials that have been deleted or altered in the past year, or are willing to share how those changes affect you, we’d love to hear from you. Please reach out at deleted-data@theguardian.com . https://www.dw.com/en/tunisia-judge-orde.text: Skip to content Skip to main menu Skip to more DW sites https://p.dw.com/p/5Le7e Tunisians took to the streets in August to call for the release of jailed activists and journalists and the president's resignation Image: Jihed Abidellaoui/REUTERS Advertisement A judge in Tunisia ordered the detention of prominent journalist Mohamed Yousfi on Friday. Police had taken him into custody as he arrived at a radio station to give an interview, according to Zied Dabbar, president of the journalist syndicate SNJT. Dabbar said it was unclear why Yousfi was detained outside Radio Express FM , but he believed it was related to Yousfi's criticism of the authorities. The judge ordered Yousfi detained on charges of illicit enrichment and money laundering, the state news agency reported, citing a judicial source. No reason provided for detention Yousfi, editor-in-chief of investigative news website Al-Qatiba, has been an outspoken critic of President Kais Saied. Al-Qatiba is known for investigative reporting and coverage of political, economic, social and environmental issues. Radio Express FM host Walid Ben Rhouma said no reason was given for Yousfi's detention. "He was barred from entering to participate in the program as a guest and was taken away for questioning, according to those who stopped him," Rhouma said in a Facebook post. The SNJT said Yousfi's detention shows the erosion of press freedoms in Tunisia , where reporters, lawyers, opposition figures and activists have recently faced prosecution. Attack on freedom of the press SNJT called Yousfi's arrest not only an attack on him but also on all journalists and Tunisians' right to a free and independent media. Rights ⁠groups ​warn of efforts to close Tunisia's remaining independent ​voices since Saied suspended parliament in 2021 and dissolved it in 2022. Saied says he will not be a dictator and that freedoms are guaranteed in Tunisia. In August, protesters took the streets to demonstrate in support of jailed activists and journalists, as well as to call for Saied's removal from power. Media figures jailed this year include Zied Heni, Mourad Zghidi and Borhen Bsaies. Khaoula Boukrim was sentenced in June to four years in ​absentia. On Thursday, lawyer Ghazi Mrabet, known for handling politically sensitive and civil liberties cases, was arrested and placed in custody, according to local media reports. The case reportedly involves alleged drug trafficking, although there are conflicting accounts of the circumstances. https://english.republika.mk/world/hunga.text: Hungary, a country known for its large rivers, lakes and spas, is facing an unusual and worrying situation this summer – water is literally disappearing in many places. The long-term drought and extremely high temperatures have seriously affected the country’s water resources. The level of rivers and lakes has dropped, and in some places the water has receded so much that it has left behind cracked earth, parched shores and landscapes that look more like southern Europe at the height of a drought than a central European country. The situation at Lake Velence, one of Hungary’s most famous lakes, has attracted particular attention, where the water level has dropped to an exceptionally low level. In parts of the shore, the water has receded hundreds of meters, and places that are usually crowded with swimmers and tourists have been left with an almost completely dry riverbed. There are also problems on the Danube. The low water level not only creates difficulties for navigation and agriculture, but also reveals parts of the riverbed that have been hidden under water for years. Among them is the so-called “Famine Rock” – a rock that, according to local legends, becames visible during periods of extreme drought and poor harvests. Its reappearance due to the low level of the Danube was seen by the public as another warning of the seriousness of the situation. The drought is already having an impact on agriculture. Farmers are facing damaged crops and water shortages, while high temperatures are further accelerating the evaporation of water from lakes and rivers. Scientists and experts warn that Hungary, although traditionally considered a country rich in water, is becoming increasingly sensitive to long dry periods and extreme weather conditions. The image of dried-up banks and rivers revealing parts of their old beds is perhaps the best symbol of this summer in Hungary – a country through which major European rivers flow, and which is now facing a much simpler but serious question: what will happen if the water continues to disappear? Photograph: Serhii Dilin/EPA View image in fullscreen Ukrainian rescuers work at the site of a Russian strike on a medical centre in central Kyiv, Ukraine, 28 September 2026, amid the Russian invasion. Photograph: Serhii Dilin/EPA Russia-Ukraine war at a glance Ukraine Explainer Ukraine war briefing: Nato condemns Moscow’s ‘irresponsible nuclear rhetoric’ as strikes on Kyiv intensify Comments come after Moscow warned it would ‘deploy its entire arsenal’ if Kaliningrad was threatened. What we know on day 1,680 Guardian staff and agencies Tue 29 Sep 2026 22.22 EDT Last modified on Tue 29 Sep 2026 22.33 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google Nato on Tuesday condemned “irresponsible nuclear rhetoric” by Russia, after Moscow warned it would “deploy its entire arsenal” if the alliance threatens its exclave Kaliningrad. “I can confirm that Russia sent a non-paper to Nato and that we have sent a response, noting that Nato is a defensive Alliance and none of our activities or exercises pose a risk to any part of Russia,” Allison Hart, a Nato spokesperson, said. “We strongly denounce the threat of force, including any irresponsible nuclear rhetoric. We call on Russia to end its unprovoked war in Ukraine .” Russia has intensified daytime strikes on Kyiv using jet-powered drones that Ukrainian forces are struggling to intercept . Russia fired ballistic missiles and dozens of jet-powered drones at Kyiv, Ukraine’s air force said Tuesday, as Moscow seeks to make Ukraine buckle under the pressure of day-and-night bombardment of its capital and other cities. Russia has used new jet-powered drones that fly too fast and too high for Ukrainian ground-based air defenses to shoot down. Russia struck ⁠two datacentres ⁠in ​Kyiv overnight, a military-linked ⁠cargo vessel in the Black Sea, and ⁠another vessel with ​military ‌cargo ‌in the Ukrainian port ‌of Odesa , the Russian defence ministry said on Tuesday. In a later evening statement, ‌the ministry said its forces had ​launched a drone strike on a ship in ⁠the Black Sea ​which it said ​was ​carrying cargo intended ​for ‌the ​Ukrainian ​armed forces. Ukraine’s top university on Tuesday said it was ordering students to stay home as it switched to remote classes due to the surge in Russian daytime drone attacks on the capital. Kyiv’s Taras Shevchenko National University said it would “switch to a remote format of work” until at least 16 October, “due to the deteriorating security situation in Kyiv”. The university’s main campus is close to the National Academy of Sciences, which was hit by a drone strike, killing one person, on Monday. Russian glide bombs ⁠struck a school in the northern ⁠Ukrainian ⁠city of ​Sumy on Tuesday, killing ⁠two people and injuring six , the regional ⁠governor said. The city’s governor, Oleh ​Hryhorov, said three children ‌were among the injured. He said teachers and school officials had managed to ‌evacuate 100 people. View image in fullscreen Kirill Dmitriev, Russia’s presidential envoy on foreign investment and economic cooperation, met with US officials in Washington to discuss post-war energy projects. He is pictured in Moscow last month. Photograph: Gavriil Grigorov/Reuters Russia’s foreign investment envoy, Kirill Dmitriev, met US officials in Washington for talks about future US-Russia energy projects planned after Moscow’s war against Ukraine , a US government official told AFP. Dmitriev and US officials held “constructive discussions on a peaceful resolution to the Russia-Ukraine conflict and possible US-Russia energy initiatives after the war ends” on Monday, the official said on Tuesday. “The visit follows special envoy Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner’s recent meeting with president Putin in Moscow and their discussions last week with Ukrainian officials in NYC,” said the official, speaking anonymously. The US president, Donald Trump, favours a proposal under which the US would lift some sanctions if Russia released a number of political prisoners , according to a report in the Atlantic. The White House did not comment directly on the report. When asked about the article, a US official told AFP that Trump was “committed to continuing to play a constructive role in ending the war between Russia and Ukraine, and he remains optimistic that we’ll ultimately get a peace deal done”. Russia will cut funding for welfare, education and healthcare in next year’s state budget to help cover soaring military spending , fiscal documents obtained by Reuters showed. Russia plans to spend 17.1tn ⁠roubles (US$202.58bn) on defence in ⁠2027, about 27% more than the 13.5tn roubles originally budgeted and the highest figure since the start of the war in Ukraine in ⁠2022. Funding for social policy, which covers items such as state pensions, payments to war veterans and maternity benefits, will shrink by 7%, while education funding will fall by 6% and healthcare by 6.8%. Belgium will transfer three F-16 fighter jets to Ukraine by the end ⁠of the ⁠year ​to help in its war with Russia , Ukraine’s president, Volodymyr Zelenskyy, said on Tuesday. Zelenskyy said Ukraine had already received “urgent deliveries” of F-16 ‌ammunition from Belgium and Spain, among other countries. Zelenskyy later said later Ukraine had received a “very good” assistance package the day before of a NASAMS air defence system, ‌developed jointly in the US and Norway. A Russian nuclear-capable strategic bomber crashed Tuesday on a training mission in the country’s far east, killing six members of its crew , its defence ministry said. The ministry said in a statement that the Tu-95 bomber went down in an unpopulated area in the Amur region, adding that one crew member survived the crash and was hospitalised with injuries. https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cw5y.text: Figure caption, By Jacob Phillips Published 20 October 2026, 07:35 BST Updated 1 hour ago A suspect linked to a far-left movement has been arrested in France after a 19th Century city hall was gutted by a fire over the weekend that broke out during mass disorder, French media report. The clock tower and parts of the roof of the ornate city hall in the central city of Limoges were engulfed in flames before collapsing on Saturday. The 40-year-old suspect is known for acts of violence against public officials and has been classified as an "S" subject, meaning he is a potential threat to national security, FranceInfo reported. More than 120 people have already been imprisoned following widespread demonstrations across France, French Justice Minister GÃ©rald Darmanin told CNews-Europe. Hundreds of thousands of demonstrators took to the streets to protest against rising fuel prices, the cost of living and deteriorating public services, including schools. Darmanin said he asked prosecutors to be "extremely firm" and "ruthless towards those who attacked police officers, gendarmes and firefighters, who looted shops and who attacked public buildings". The justice minister insisted France did not need to be put into a state of emergency which would "deprive all French people of their individual freedoms". But French Prime Minister SÃ©bastien Lecornu earlier said he had not ruled out imposing a state of emergency. Image source, AFP via Getty Images Image caption, The city hall's roof and clock tower in Limoges was severely damaged in the fire Targeted curfews introduced across France on Monday contributed to a quiet night following the disorder, Lecornu said. Curfews were introduced across parts of central Paris, including Place de la RÃ©publique, where protesters had gathered over the weekend, and the Les Halles shopping area. Other measures restricting the movement of young people and gatherings were introduced in cities such as Marseille, Bordeaux, Nice and Lyon in the south, as well as Lille and other towns in the north. Lecornu thanked police officers and gendarmes for enforcing the measures, adding that further curfews on Tuesday night would be decided depending on where they were necessary. Writing in a post on X, he said decisions would be made "on the ground" by French regions and local mayors. Image source, Anadolu via Getty Images Image caption, The streets in the southern city of Lyon were quiet on Monday night Earlier Interior Minister Laurent NuÃ±ez admitted police had "lost control" in some cities. He was strongly criticised by opposition politicians over authorities' preparedness for the disorder, leading him to offer his resignation on Monday, which was rejected by President Emmanuel Macron. More than 2,500 people have been arrested since the disorder broke out, officials said on Monday. One demonstrator's hand was blown off by a police crowd-control grenade, according to the AFP news agency. About 1,000 police officers were injured. Protests first began last month with students demanding better school conditions but they have escalated to take in a broader range of concerns with numbers at demonstrations bolstered by trade unions and various protest groups. Image source, Reuters Image caption, Riots took place across French cities, including the capital Paris More than 2,000 shops and other businesses have been directly impacted by the weekend's violence, the head of France's Chambers of Commerce and Industry (CCI) said. Rioters, some dressed in black and wearing masks and balaclavas, were seen setting fire to cars and buildings and looting businesses in Paris, Marseille and other cities and smaller towns. Protest organisers have declared that a second round of protests will take place on Saturday across France. The so-called yellow vests (gilets jaunes), who were responsible for France's longest-ever modern protests in 2018, has said "Act II" will take place this weekend.
